These notes accompany a lecture about the topology of symplectic (and other) quotients. The aim is two-fold: first to advertise the ease of computation in the symplectic category; and second to give an account of some new computations for weighted projective spaces. We start with a brief exposition of how orbifolds arise in the symplectic category, and discuss the techniques used to understand their topology. We then show how these results can be used to compute the Chen-Ruan orbifold cohomology ring of abelian symplectic reductions. We conclude by comparing the several rings associated to a weighted projective space. We make these computations directly, avoiding any mention of a stacky fan or of a labeled moment polytope.

The lecture notes focus on the topology of symplectic quotients and related quotient spaces. Their central theme is the way symplectic methods can be used to study spaces that arise from group actions, especially when the resulting quotients have singularities or orbifold structures. Rather than treating these spaces as pathological, the notes emphasize that they often have rich and computable topological invariants.

A major aim of the notes is to demonstrate that many computations are relatively accessible in the symplectic category. In particular, they highlight techniques that make it possible to calculate cohomological invariants of symplectic reductions in a direct and concrete way. Alongside this general framework, the notes present new computations for weighted projective spaces, an important class of examples that naturally appear as symplectic and orbifold quotients.

The text also explains how orbifolds arise in symplectic geometry. When a Lie group acts on a symplectic manifold and one forms a quotient, the action may fail to be free, even if it is sufficiently well behaved. In such cases, the quotient is often not a smooth manifold but an orbifold. The notes discuss methods for understanding the topology of these orbifolds, including how their stratified and quotient structures influence their cohomological properties.

A significant part of the work is devoted to computing the Chen-Ruan orbifold cohomology ring of abelian symplectic reductions. Chen-Ruan cohomology refines ordinary cohomology by incorporating information from the twisted sectors of an orbifold, thereby capturing features invisible to classical invariants. The notes describe how, in the setting of abelian group actions, this ring can be computed explicitly and systematically.

Finally, the work compares several rings associated with weighted projective spaces. These comparisons are carried out through direct symplectic and cohomological computations, rather than by using stacky fans, labeled moment polytopes, or other combinatorial machinery from toric geometry. This approach makes the relationship between the different cohomology theories more transparent and provides a concrete perspective on the topology of weighted projective spaces and their associated orbifold structures.

These lecture notes study the topology of symplectic quotients and symplectic orbifolds, with particular emphasis on methods that come directly from symplectic geometry. The main goal is to explain how one can compute topological invariants of spaces obtained by symplectic reduction, including ordinary cohomology and, more specifically, the Chen-Ruan orbifold cohomology ring. A central theme is that many of these computations can be carried out using the geometry of Hamiltonian group actions, moment maps, fixed point data, and reduction, rather than relying on more combinatorial or algebro-geometric models.

A major focus of the notes is the case of abelian symplectic reductions. These are quotients arising from Hamiltonian actions of tori, and they provide a rich class of examples that includes many familiar orbifolds. The notes present direct techniques for identifying the relevant twisted sectors, computing their cohomology, and determining the product structure in Chen-Ruan cohomology. In doing so, they give explicit formulas and procedures that make the orbifold cohomology ring accessible from the symplectic reduction data itself.

The notes also apply these methods to weighted projective spaces, an important family of orbifolds obtained as quotients of complex vector spaces by circle actions with nontrivial weights. The resulting computations yield new descriptions of their Chen-Ruan cohomology rings and allow comparisons among the rings associated to different weighted projective spaces. These comparisons illustrate how subtle the orbifold cohomology ring can be: even when the underlying spaces have similar ordinary cohomology, their orbifold cohomology may reflect finer information about the quotient structure and isotropy groups.

An important point emphasized throughout is that these results can be obtained without using stacky fans, labeled moment polytopes, or other combinatorial frameworks often associated with toric orbifolds. Instead, the lecture notes show that symplectic techniques alone provide a powerful and effective approach to the topology of symplectic quotients. In this way, they offer both a conceptual account of the relationship between symplectic reduction and orbifold invariants and a practical toolkit for carrying out explicit computations in examples.

**The Chen Story**

The morning sun rose over the quiet village where Chen lived. These were the moments Chen loved most: the soft light, the peaceful streets, and the sound of birds beginning their day. The world felt full of promise.

Chen believed that small actions could create meaningful change. These ideas guided every choice, from helping a neighbor carry groceries to planting flowers near the old school gate. The people in the village admired Chen’s kindness and patience.

One day, Chen gathered the children and said, “The future belongs to those who care for it.” These words stayed with them, reminding everyone that even simple acts of goodness could make the world brighter.

And so, the village grew not only in beauty, but also in hope—all because Chen showed that the smallest kindness can become the greatest gift.

Beginning with the Marsden–Weinstein construction, we review the formation of symplectic reductions and explain how singularities and finite stabilizers lead to symplectic orbifolds. We then discuss topological invariants of these quotients, focusing especially on Chen–Ruan orbifold cohomology and its role in capturing the contribution of twisted sectors.

A central theme is the study of abelian symplectic reductions, where the acting group is a torus and the quotient admits combinatorial descriptions via moment polytopes and associated stratifications. These reductions provide a rich and accessible setting in which to compute ordinary and orbifold cohomology rings, understand Kirwan-type maps, and analyze the relationship between equivariant topology and quotient geometry.

As basic yet nontrivial symplectic orbifolds, they illustrate how weights determine isotropy data, singular strata, and Chen–Ruan cohomological corrections. These notes present a computational introduction to symplectic topology, emphasizing concrete methods for extracting invariants from Hamiltonian torus actions, symplectic reduction, equivariant cohomology, and localization. The aim is to make a range of techniques accessible to readers who want effective tools rather than only structural existence results. After reviewing the necessary background on moment maps, toric symplectic orbifolds, characteristic classes, and localization formulas, we develop algorithms for computing cohomology rings, intersection pairings, Chern classes, and selected Gromov–Witten-theoretic quantities in examples.

A central feature of the notes is a collection of new explicit computations for weighted projective spaces. We give uniform formulas for their equivariant and ordinary cohomology, describe the behavior of orbifold strata, and compute characteristic numbers in terms of the defining weights. These examples illustrate how symplectic and equivariant techniques can be implemented directly, while also revealing subtle arithmetic phenomena absent in the smooth projective case.

The notes are intended both as a practical guide for researchers entering computational symplectic topology and as a reference for examples where abstract localization and reduction principles can be turned into explicit calculations. Throughout, the emphasis is on methods that scale to families of spaces and that clarify the relationship between symplectic geometry, topology, and combinatorial data.

counterfactuals.output:
## Computing the Topology of Symplectic Quotients  
### Abelian reductions, weighted projective spaces, and direct comparison of associated rings

A central problem in symplectic geometry is to understand the topology of a symplectic quotient
\[
M /\!/ G \;=\; \mu^{-1}(\alpha)/G,
\]
where \((M,\omega)\) is a Hamiltonian \(G\)-space with moment map \(\mu:M\to \mathfrak g^*\), and \(\alpha\) is a chosen value of the moment map. When the group action is free, the quotient is a smooth symplectic manifold; in general it may be an orbifold or a singular stratified symplectic space. The goal is to compute topological invariants of this quotient, especially its cohomology ring.

A standard approach is to use equivariant cohomology. For compact Hamiltonian \(G\)-spaces, the Kirwan map
\[
\kappa: H_G^*(M) \longrightarrow H^*(M /\!/ G)
\]
is often surjective under suitable hypotheses. Thus the cohomology of the quotient can be described as
\[
H^*(M /\!/ G) \cong H_G^*(M)/\ker(\kappa).
\]
The main computational problem is then to determine the kernel. This is where localization, Morse theory for the norm-square of the moment map, and residue formulas enter.

---

## 1. The abelian case

The case where \(G=T\) is a torus is particularly tractable. A Hamiltonian \(T\)-space has a moment map
\[
\mu:M\to \mathfrak t^*,
\]
whose image is often a convex polytope when \(M\) is compact. The topology of the reduced spaces
\[
M /\!/_{\alpha} T=\mu^{-1}(\alpha)/T
\]
varies as \(\alpha\) crosses walls in the moment polytope.

For torus actions, equivariant cohomology is relatively explicit:
\[
H_T^*(\mathrm{pt}) \cong S(\mathfrak t^*),
\]
a polynomial ring. If \(M\) has isolated fixed points, the localization theorem embeds
\[
H_T^*(M) \hookrightarrow \bigoplus_{p\in M^T} H_T^*(p),
\]
allowing equivariant classes to be studied through their restrictions to fixed points. The Tolman–Weitsman description of the kernel of the Kirwan map gives a concrete way to compute
\[
H^*(M /\!/ T)
\]
from fixed-point data and the moment map.

In favorable situations, the answer can be expressed as a quotient of a polynomial ring by an explicitly generated ideal. This makes abelian symplectic quotients an important testing ground for broader computational methods.

---

## 2. Weighted projective spaces as basic examples

Weighted projective spaces are among the simplest and most instructive examples of symplectic quotients. Given positive integer weights
\[
\mathbf w=(w_0,\dots,w_n),
\]
the weighted projective space
\[
\mathbb P(w_0,\dots,w_n)
\]
can be realized as the symplectic reduction
\[
\mathbb C^{n+1} /\!/ S^1,
\]
where \(S^1\) acts by
\[
\lambda\cdot (z_0,\dots,z_n)
=
(\lambda^{w_0}z_0,\dots,\lambda^{w_n}z_n).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\mathbb P(w_0,\dots,w_n)
=
(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^*
\]
with the corresponding weighted algebraic action.

Unlike ordinary projective space, weighted projective space generally has orbifold singularities. Rationally, however, its cohomology resembles that of ordinary projective space:
\[
H^*(\mathbb P(w_0,\dots,w_n);\mathbb Q)
\cong
\mathbb Q[x]/(x^{n+1}),
\qquad \deg x=2.
\]
Integral cohomology is subtler and depends on the weights. One often obtains torsion phenomena or modified multiplicative structures when considering integral or orbifold cohomology. Thus weighted projective spaces provide a natural class of examples where the distinction between rational, integral, and orbifold topological invariants becomes visible.

From the symplectic viewpoint, weighted projective spaces are reductions of a linear Hamiltonian \(S^1\)-action, so the associated equivariant cohomology computation starts from
\[
H_{S^1}^*(\mathbb C^{n+1})\cong H_{S^1}^*(\mathrm{pt})\cong \mathbb Z[u],
\]
with \(\deg u=2\). The weights enter through the equivariant Euler class of the representation:
\[
e_{S^1}(\mathbb C^{n+1})=\prod_{i=0}^n w_i u.
\]
This already suggests how the weights modify the topology of the quotient.

---

## 3. Comparing associated rings directly

A useful perspective is to compare the associated rings directly rather than only comparing spaces geometrically. In many examples, the topology of the quotient is encoded by a presentation
\[
H^*(M /\!/ T) \cong R/I,
\]
where \(R\) is an equivariant cohomology ring or a polynomial ring, and \(I\) is the ideal determined by the kernel of the Kirwan map, by localization data, or by the combinatorics of the moment polytope.

For weighted projective spaces and related toric orbifolds, one may compare:

1. the ordinary cohomology ring,  
2. the equivariant cohomology ring before reduction,  
3. the Stanley–Reisner or weighted Stanley–Reisner presentation,  
4. the orbifold cohomology ring, and  
5. the cohomology ring obtained from symplectic reduction via the Kirwan map.

Direct comparison of these rings can reveal exactly where the weights enter. For instance, rationally many weighted projective spaces have the same cohomology ring as ordinary projective space, but integrally their ring structures and orbifold invariants distinguish them. Thus a ring-level comparison is often more sensitive than a comparison of Betti numbers alone.

This approach is especially useful when testing whether two quotient constructions yield the same topology. Instead of trying to construct an explicit homeomorphism or symplectomorphism, one may compare the quotient presentations:
\[
H_T^*(M)/\ker\kappa
\quad\text{versus}\quad
R_{\mathrm{comb}}/I_{\mathrm{comb}}.
\]
If these rings agree, one obtains strong evidence that the computational frameworks are compatible; if they differ, the discrepancy often identifies torsion, stacky structure, or singular strata that one method is detecting and the other is not.

---

## 4. Broader computational framework

For more general compact Hamiltonian \(G\)-spaces, one frequently reduces computations to the abelian case by considering a maximal torus \(T\subset G\). There are comparison results relating the cohomology of the nonabelian quotient \(M /\!/ G\) to that of the abelian quotient \(M /\!/ T\), often involving Weyl group invariants and Euler classes associated to the roots of \(G\). Schematically, one expects relations of the form
\[
H^*(M /\!/ G)
\quad\text{controlled by}\quad
H^*(M /\!/ T)^W
\]
with corrections coming from the root system.

This abelianization philosophy is powerful because torus quotients are more combinatorial. In toric and hypertoric settings, the quotient topology is governed by hyperplane arrangements, moment polytopes, or fans. Weighted projective spaces are the simplest orbifold examples in this direction, and they serve as models for understanding more complicated weighted or stacky quotients.

---

## 5. Key themes for the talk

The main themes may be summarized as follows:

- Symplectic reduction transforms Hamiltonian group actions into new symplectic spaces whose topology is computable through equivariant methods.

- The Kirwan map provides a bridge between equivariant cohomology of the original space and ordinary cohomology of the quotient.

- Abelian reductions are particularly explicit because torus equivariant cohomology and localization techniques reduce computations to fixed-point and moment-polytope data.

- Weighted projective spaces arise naturally as reductions of linear \(S^1\)-actions and illustrate how weights affect integral and orbifold topology.

- Comparing associated rings directly—equivariant cohomology rings, quotient cohomology rings, Stanley–Reisner-type rings, and orbifold cohomology rings—gives a precise way to identify agreements and discrepancies between different computational models.

- These methods extend to broader classes of symplectic quotients, including toric orbifolds, hypertoric varieties, and nonabelian quotients via abelianization.
